Family Health

Paratubal and paraovarian cysts: symptoms and care

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A paratubal or paraovarian cyst is a sac near a fallopian tube or ovary, rather than a cyst growing within the ovary itself. Many are fluid-filled, harmless and discovered incidentally. Care depends on the actual appearance, symptoms and clinical circumstances; finding a cyst does not automatically mean that surgery is needed.

What these cysts are: and are not

The terms overlap: “paraovarian” means beside the ovary and “paratubal” beside the fallopian tube. They develop in nearby tissue, often within the broad ligament supporting the reproductive organs. They are not simply unattached sacs floating in the abdomen. Some contain tissue as well as fluid, which affects assessment.

They can occur at different ages and range from tiny incidental findings to larger masses. Because many cause no symptoms, their frequency is difficult to measure. Unlike functional ovarian cysts associated with ovulation, they are nonfunctional: do not assume they will disappear with the next few periods. Persistence alone does not mean cancer or require an operation.

Symptoms and reasons to seek assessment

A small uncomplicated cyst may cause no symptoms and be found during an examination, ultrasound or unrelated surgery. A larger cyst can cause pelvic or lower abdominal discomfort, fullness, pain during sex, constipation or urinary pressure. These symptoms have other possible causes; an existing cyst does not explain every new pain.

Arrange assessment for persistent or recurring pain, bloating, early fullness, bowel or urinary changes, or unusual vaginal bleeding. Do not assume bleeding comes from the cyst. Seek urgent assessment now for pelvic pain with fever, vomiting, unusual vaginal bleeding, unusual discharge, difficulty passing urine or stool, or pregnancy or possible pregnancy.

How they form

Some cysts arise from tissue left over from fetal development, including Müllerian (paramesonephric) or Wolffian (mesonephric) duct remnants. These ducts are involved in early reproductive-system development. Fluid can collect within nearby tissues; the precise origin of an individual cyst may only become clear after examination of removed tissue.

There is no established lifestyle measure that prevents these cysts, and no reason to blame yourself for developing one. Age patterns in reported cases do not mean they occur only between 30 and 40, or that a large cyst in a younger person is necessarily dangerous. They are not an ordinary monthly ovulation follicle.

Examination and ultrasound

A clinician reviews the pain, menstrual history, possibility of pregnancy, previous imaging and relevant medical or family history. Examination and a pregnancy test may be appropriate. Pelvic ultrasound usually helps locate the cyst in relation to the ovary and tube, measure it and assess whether it looks simple or complex.

An abdominal scan may be used; a transvaginal scan can provide more detail when suitable and accepted after explanation and consent. Discuss an alternative if it is unsuitable or you do not want it. Sometimes imaging cannot confidently distinguish a paraovarian cyst from another adnexal mass, so further specialist assessment is needed.

What MRI, blood tests and laparoscopy can tell you

MRI may help characterize a mass that ultrasound cannot fully assess. Blood tests are selected for the situation: a blood count can assess anaemia or infection concerns, while tumour markers may contribute to a cancer-risk assessment. Neither MRI nor a tumour-marker result alone proves or rules out cancer. Most simple paraovarian cysts are benign; concerning features need specialist review.

Laparoscopy uses small abdominal cuts and a camera to inspect the pelvis, often while treating a problem. It is not a required diagnostic test for every incidental cyst. If tissue is removed, laboratory examination can establish its type. Suspected torsion is a different, urgent situation: assessment and treatment must not be delayed for repeated routine scans.

Observation or surgery: an individual decision

If the cyst is clearly simple, causes no symptoms and has a low risk of complications, no treatment (and sometimes no routine follow-up) may be appropriate. Other cases need planned ultrasound surveillance. Ask whether follow-up is needed, when it should happen and which symptoms should trigger earlier contact. Observation does not promise spontaneous disappearance.

Surgery may be considered for troublesome symptoms, growth, uncertain or concerning imaging, or a significant complication risk. Size matters alongside appearance, age, menopausal status, health and your preferences; there is no universal “over 10 cm means surgery” rule. Smaller cysts can also need urgent treatment if they twist or bleed. Hormonal pills are not a proven way to dissolve a paraovarian cyst.

Cyst removal and recovery

Cystectomy means removing the cyst while aiming to preserve healthy nearby structures. Laparoscopy is keyhole surgery; laparotomy uses a larger abdominal opening and may be chosen for a very large or concerning mass or other surgical needs. These operations generally use general anaesthesia, rather than being routine procedures under local anaesthetic.

Discuss the planned approach, possible changes during surgery, bleeding, infection, injury to nearby organs and anaesthetic risks. Keyhole surgery often allows a quicker recovery, but recovery varies with the operation and individual health. Follow the discharge plan and seek prompt advice for fever or offensive discharge. Severe or worsening pain, heavy bleeding, faintness or breathing difficulty require immediate emergency care.

Torsion, rupture and pressure complications

Torsion is twisting of the cyst and sometimes the fallopian tube, ovary or their supporting structures, potentially cutting off blood supply. Sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, often with nausea or vomiting, needs immediate emergency assessment, even if pain comes and goes. Normal Doppler blood flow does not by itself exclude torsion. Prompt surgery aims to untwist and preserve tissue when possible, but preservation cannot be guaranteed.

A ruptured cyst can cause internal bleeding; treatment depends on the symptoms and stability, rather than every rupture requiring surgery. Rare very large cysts can compress the bladder, bowel, uterus or urinary drainage pathways. Obstructed drainage can cause hydronephrosis, swelling of the kidney from backed-up urine. Tube damage or, rarely, rupture can occur with severe complications; these are possibilities, not expected outcomes for every small cyst.

Fertility and the outlook

An uncomplicated small cyst usually does not interfere with ovulation or prevent pregnancy. A large mass, torsion, tubal damage, the underlying condition and the operation can affect fertility. Tell the team about future pregnancy plans before planned surgery. Early emergency treatment offers a chance to protect function; it cannot promise preservation of an ovary or tube.

Sometimes removal of an ovary (oophorectomy), a tube (salpingectomy) or both is necessary. Pregnancy may remain possible with a healthy remaining ovary and functioning tube, but chances depend on the whole situation. Many people need only reassurance or monitoring. Do not replace follow-up with a promise that all cysts disappear, that every large cyst needs removal or that fertility is always unaffected.

When pain is an emergency

Get immediate emergency care for severe or worsening pelvic pain, sudden intense pain with nausea or vomiting, fainting or marked dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, confusion or heavy vaginal bleeding. These can signal torsion, significant bleeding or another emergency. Do not drive yourself if faint or seriously unwell.

Pelvic pain with possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment even without a positive test, because ectopic pregnancy is another possible cause. Severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, faintness or heavy bleeding makes this an immediate emergency. A known cyst must not delay assessment of a new or worsening symptom; do not wait for a scheduled scan or a particular cyst size.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

July 2026 Cleveland Clinic information supports individualized assessment and care for cysts beside the ovary or tube.

The SRU consensus distinguishes paraovarian cysts from normal follicles. Follow-up decisions for these nonfunctional cysts should account for symptoms, imaging features and individual circumstances.

Available RCOG and NHS surgical information supports discussing imaging, anaesthesia, operative risks and fertility; MRI or markers alone are not a cancer diagnosis.

ACOG torsion guidance and current NHS pelvic-pain advice support prompt emergency assessment and organ-preserving treatment when possible, without a guarantee.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record pain, bleeding, menstrual dates, urinary or bowel changes, scan findings and questions about follow-up or fertility. A record cannot identify the cyst type, exclude cancer or torsion, or replace urgent assessment.

When to seek help

Do not try to press, drain or treat a cyst yourself, or use hormones to dissolve it without medical advice. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, sudden pain with vomiting, fainting, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or heavy bleeding needs immediate emergency care. Possible pregnancy with pelvic pain needs urgent assessment; severe symptoms make it an immediate emergency. Do not wait for the next scan or assume every new symptom is from a known cyst.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Paratubal and paraovarian cysts develop beside the ovary or tube and are usually benign.
  • They are nonfunctional cysts; routine disappearance over a few menstrual cycles cannot be assumed.
  • Ultrasound guides assessment; MRI and tumour markers cannot independently diagnose cancer.
  • Observation, follow-up or surgery depends on the full clinical picture, not a single size threshold.
  • Sudden severe pain, fainting or heavy bleeding needs immediate emergency care; fertility preservation is an aim, not a guarantee.

Frequently asked questions

What causes a paratubal cyst?

It can arise from nearby tissue or embryonic duct remnants, including Müllerian or Wolffian remnants. There is no established preventive lifestyle measure, and its presence is not your fault.

Will it disappear by itself?

Do not assume so. These are nonfunctional cysts, unlike many ovulation-related ovarian cysts. A stable simple cyst may still be harmless and need no treatment; your clinician decides whether surveillance is needed.

Which symptoms can it cause?

Many cause none. Larger or complicated cysts may cause pelvic pain, fullness, bowel or urinary pressure or pain during sex. Other conditions can cause the same symptoms, so new or persistent symptoms need assessment.

Can MRI or a blood test confirm cancer?

No single MRI or tumour-marker result establishes or excludes cancer. Clinicians combine history and imaging with selected tests and, when appropriate, specialist assessment and examination of removed tissue.

Does a cyst over 10 cm always need surgery?

No universal cutoff applies. Symptoms, growth, appearance, complication risk, age, health and preferences all matter. A very large cyst needs specialist assessment, while even a smaller cyst can need emergency treatment for torsion.

How is it removed?

Often by keyhole cystectomy, with general anaesthesia, aiming to preserve healthy structures. A larger opening may be needed in selected cases. Discuss the risks, recovery and possibility of removing a tube or ovary before planned surgery.

Will my fertility be preserved?

Many uncomplicated cysts do not affect fertility. Treatment aims to preserve the ovary and tube where safe, but cannot guarantee this. Pregnancy may still be possible with one healthy ovary and functioning tube; individual circumstances matter.

Which complications need immediate help?

Sudden severe or worsening pelvic pain, especially with vomiting, faintness, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait for a scan, a large size or every warning sign. Possible pregnancy with pelvic pain needs urgent assessment too.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
